claim: A large-scale optogenetic interface enabled simultaneous stimulation of excitatory neurons and electrocorticographic recording across primary somatosensory (S1) and motor (M1) cortex.
source: A large-scale optogenetic interface enabled simultaneous stimulation of excitatory neurons and electrocorticographic recording across primary somatosensory (S1) and motor (M1) cortex (Yazdan-Shahmorad et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to prior work (Yazdan-Shahmorad et al., 2016) and is described as a method used in the current study.

claim: The network response to focal stimulation and the baseline coherence between pairs of electrodes were strongly correlated before stimulation.
source: We tracked two measures of network connectivity, the network response to focal stimulation and the baseline coherence between pairs of electrodes; these were strongly correlated before stimulation.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data presented in Figure 3.

claim: Within minutes, stimulation in S1 or M1 significantly strengthened the gross functional connectivity between these areas.
source: Within minutes, stimulation in S1 or M1 significantly strengthened the gross functional connectivity between these areas.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data shown in Figures 4 and 5.

claim: Stimulation led to heterogeneous connectivity changes across the network.
source: At a finer scale, stimulation led to heterogeneous connectivity changes across the network.
evidence: The claim is stated in the abstract and supported by data in Figure 6A showing varied changes across recording sites.

claim: The connectivity changes reflected the correlations introduced by stimulation-evoked activity, consistent with Hebbian plasticity models.
source: These changes reflected the correlations introduced by stimulation-evoked activity, consistent with Hebbian plasticity models.
evidence: The claim is stated in the abstract and supported by regression analysis in Figures 6 and 7 showing correlation between stimulus-evoked coherence and changes in baseline coherence.

claim: Many neurological and psychiatric disorders arise from dysfunctional neural dynamics at the network level, which in turn stem from aberrant neural connectivity.
source: Many neurological and psychiatric disorders arise from dysfunctional neural dynamics at the network level, which in turn stem from aberrant neural connectivity (Stam, 2014; Wu et al., 2016; Edwardson et al., 2013; Yahata et al., 2016; DeSalvo et al., 2014; Skudlarski et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: The brain shows marked plasticity across a variety of learning and memory tasks.
source: The brain shows marked plasticity across a variety of learning and memory tasks (Takeuchi et al., 2014; Bliss et al., 2014)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The brain shows marked plasticity during recovery after brain injury or stroke.
source: The brain shows marked plasticity across a variety of learning and memory tasks (Takeuchi et al., 2014; Bliss et al., 2014) and during recovery after brain injury or stroke (Edwardson et al., 2013; Hara, 2015; Murphy and Corbett, 2009)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The simple Hebbian model of plasticity and spike-timing dependent versions of it explain a large body of data on activity-dependent plasticity.
source: The simple Hebbian model of plasticity (Donald, 1949) and spike-timing dependent versions of it (Bi and Poo , 2001) explain a large body of data on activity-dependent plasticity, including both in vitro (Massobrio et al., 2015; Abrahamsson et al., 2016), and in vivo (Andersen et al., 2017; Feldman, 2012; Shulz and Jacob, 2010) studies.
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: The viral vector used to obtain opsin expression targeted excitatory neurons.
source: The viral vector used to obtain opsin expression targeted excitatory neurons (see supplementary material for details; Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is stated in the text and supported by histological data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Excitatory neurons have strong projections within and between M1 and S1.
source: These neurons have strong projections within and between the two brain areas (Murray and Keller, 2011; Kinnischtzke et al., 2014; Weiler et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior anatomical studies.

claim: Activating excitatory cells should increase the excitability of the underlying network, improving the likelihood of neuroplastic change.
source: Activating these excitatory cells should increase the excitability of the underlying network, improving the likelihood of neuroplastic change (Iriki et al., 1989).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation and represents a theoretical expectation based on prior work.

claim: The delays of evoked responses exhibited a bimodal distribution with a 3–6 ms separation between the early and late responses.
source: The delays exhibited a bimodal distribution with a 3–6 ms separation between the early and late responses (Figure 2B and F).
evidence: The claim is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 2B and F.

claim: Classifying the responses across electrodes by delay recovers the spatial separation between the two cortical areas—following a boundary along the central sulcus—with shorter delays in the area being stimulated and longer delays in the other area.
source: Classifying the responses across electrodes by delay recovers the spatial separation between the two cortical areas—following a boundary along the central sulcus—with shorter delays in the area being stimulated (S1 or M1; primary responses) and longer delays in the other area (M1 or S1; secondary responses) (Figure 2C and G).
evidence: The claim is stated in the text and supported by spatial maps in Figure 2C and G.

claim: The short delay of the secondary responses suggests close functional connectivity between M1 and S1.
source: The short delay of the secondary responses suggests close functional connectivity between these areas.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the observed timing of responses.

claim: SERR and coherence are derived independently from recordings with and without simultaneous stimulation.
source: Because SERR and coherence are derived independently from recordings with and without simultaneous stimulation, they might reflect fundamentally different aspects of network connectivity.
evidence: The claim describes the methodological approach used in the study.

claim: The two measures of functional connectivity (SERR and coherence) were highly correlated at baseline.
source: The two measures of functional connectivity were highly correlated: across sessions, the distribution of regression slopes was significantly different from 0 (t-test: p=3.73e-06), and 69 percent of individual experiments showed significant linear regressions (p<0.05).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of the correlation between measures.

claim: At baseline, before any conditioning, the stimulation-evoked response reflects network dynamics across the frequency spectrum.
source: This finding indicates that at baseline, before any conditioning, the stimulation-evoked response reflects network dynamics across the frequency spectrum.
evidence: The claim is an interpretation of the correlation between SERR and coherence across frequencies.

claim: Conditioning stimulation was applied for 50 min in each experiment.
source: In each experiment, conditioning stimulation was applied for 50 min, and we evaluated functional connectivity every 10 min during blocks of passive baseline recording and active testing (100 light pulses delivered through each laser).
evidence: The claim describes the experimental protocol.

claim: Stimulation in M1 leads to significant increases in mean SERR.
source: A representative example experiment, shown in Figure 4B, shows that stimulation in M1 leads to significant increases (paired t-test, p=3.88e−11) in mean SERR.
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Similar increases in SERR were observed for a majority of experiments (14 out of 18 experiments) across both monkeys.
source: Similar increases in SERR were observed for a majority of experiments (14 out of 18 experiments) across both monkeys (Figure 4C).
evidence: The claim is supported by summary data across experiments shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The increases in connectivity were symmetric between the two cortical areas.
source: The increases in connectivity were symmetric between the two cortical areas (Figure 4D).
evidence: The claim is supported by data comparing stimulation in S1 vs M1 shown in Figure 4D.

claim: No significant change in mean SERR was observed in control sessions without conditioning stimulation.
source: No significant change in mean SERR was observed in control sessions without conditioning stimulation (Figure 4D).
evidence: The claim is supported by control data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: The increase in SERR was significantly larger for stimulation sessions than control sessions.
source: Furthermore, the increase in SERR was significantly larger for stimulation sessions than control sessions (unpaired t-test: p=0.0036)
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical comparison between stimulation and control sessions.

claim: Conditioning increased mean theta band (4–8 Hz) coherence.
source: We next asked whether conditioning increased coherence-based measures of inter-area connectivity. We did observe increases in mean theta band (4–8 Hz) coherence following conditioning, as shown in Figure 4E for the same dataset used in Figure 4B (paired t-test, p=0.03).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: The increase in theta coherence was significant for the majority of experiments (13 out of 20).
source: The increase in theta coherence was significant for the majority of experiments (13 out of 20; Figure 4E)
evidence: The claim is supported by summary data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: The effect of conditioning on coherence was localized to the theta band.
source: and the effect was localized to the theta band (Figure 4G; paired t-test, p=0.017; Bonferroni correction for multiple comparisons).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis across frequency bands shown in Figure 4G.

claim: No significant changes in theta-band power were observed as a result of stimulation.
source: We also looked for change in the theta-band power as a result of stimulation and did not see any significant changes, supporting the conclusion that changes in coherence reflect changes in functional connectivity (See Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by power analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: After conditioning, the cross-channel correlation between SERR and coherence significantly decreased.
source: After conditioning, the cross-channel correlation between these measures significantly decreased (paired t-test, p=6.3e-10)
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis comparing pre- and post-conditioning correlations.

claim: The changes in SERR and coherence were uncorrelated.
source: and the changes in connectivity were uncorrelated (t-test on distribution of regression slopes, p=0.85).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of the relationship between changes in the two measures.

claim: The stimulation affects SERR and coherence differently.
source: This suggests that the stimulation affects the two measures differently.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the decreased correlation between measures after stimulation.

claim: In control (no stimulation) sessions, there was no significant decrease in the correlation between SERR and coherence.
source: In this case, we did not see a significant decrease in the correlation between measures after control sessions (paired t-test, p=0.36; see Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by control data analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: There is a trend of increasing connectivity across the session that starts within the first 10 min conditioning block.
source: For this example session (Figure 5A), and on average across all sessions (Figure 5B), there is a trend of increasing connectivity across the session that starts within the first 10 min conditioning block.
evidence: The claim is supported by temporal analysis shown in Figures 5A and 5B.

claim: The increases in inter-area connectivity measured with SERR and coherence were correlated across time.
source: These increases in inter-area connectivity measured with SERR and coherence (Figure 5B) were correlated across time (Pearson correlation coefficient = 0.26).
evidence: The claim is supported by correlation analysis of temporal dynamics.

claim: The rate of strengthening was consistent across conditioning blocks.
source: Additionally, the rate of strengthening was consistent across conditioning blocks; we detected a significant increase in SERR (p<0.05) at ~ 4.5 min of stimulation in 4 out of 5 conditioning blocks (see Figure 5—figure supplement 1 for comparison with control sessions).
evidence: The claim is supported by analysis of SERR changes within conditioning blocks.

claim: There was a significant decrease in the SERR between the last 100 pulses of the conditioning block and the following test block, indicating some unlearning of the stimulation-induced connectivity changes.
source: We did observe a significant decrease (paired t-test, p=2.9e-05) in the SERR between the last 100 pulses of the conditioning block and the following test block, indicating some unlearning of the stimulation-induced connectivity changes.
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis comparing SERR at the end of conditioning vs. test blocks.

claim: Stimulation led to heterogeneous changes in connectivity across the network.
source: This example shows heterogeneous changes in connectivity across the network.
evidence: The claim is supported by the heatmap data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: A Hebbian plasticity model suggests that the fine-scale changes in connectivity should reflect the statistics of plasticity-inducing activity.
source: A Hebbian plasticity model suggests that the fine-scale changes in connectivity should reflect the statistics of plasticity-inducing activity.
evidence: The claim is a theoretical prediction based on Hebbian plasticity principles.

claim: Correlated stimulation-evoked activity between two cortical sites would strengthen the functional connectivity between them, while uncorrelated or anti-correlated stimulation-evoked activity would weaken their functional connectivity.
source: In this case, we predicted that correlated stimulation-evoked activity between two cortical sites would strengthen the functional connectivity between them, while uncorrelated or anti-correlated stimulation-evoked activity would weaken their functional connectivity.
evidence: The claim is a prediction based on Hebbian plasticity theory.

claim: There is a similarity between the pattern of changes in baseline coherence across the array with the stimulus-evoked coherence.
source: Indeed, in the example session of Figure 6A, one can see a similarity between the pattern of changes in baseline coherence across the array (left panel) with the stimulus-evoked coherence (middle panel).
evidence: The claim is supported by visual comparison of heatmaps in Figure 6A.

claim: There is a strong correlation between the stimulus-evoked coherence and changes in baseline coherence.
source: The plot shows a strong correlation between the stimulus-evoked coherence and changes in baseline coherence.
evidence: The claim is supported by regression analysis shown in Figure 6B.

claim: The relationship between stimulus-evoked coherence and changes in baseline coherence was consistent across experimental sessions and monkeys.
source: This relationship was consistent across our data (Figure 6C): the distribution of linear regression slopes across experimental sessions and monkeys was significant (paired t-test: p=2.41e-19; 101 out of 105 experimental blocks had significant (p<0.05) linear regression models).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis across all experiments shown in Figure 6C.

claim: The results support a Hebbian model for network-wide changes in connectivity.
source: These results support a Hebbian model for network-wide changes in connectivity.
evidence: The claim is an interpretation of the correlation between stimulus-evoked coherence and connectivity changes.

claim: With interference stimulation patterns, there was no consistent increase in mean inter-area connectivity.
source: We repeated the analysis of mean inter-area coherence changes (c.f. Figure 4F) for these sessions, and we did not see a consistent increase in mean inter-area connectivity (Figure 7C).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 7C.

claim: With interference stimulation, stimulus-evoked coherence continued to predict changes in baseline coherence.
source: Nevertheless, we found that stimulus-evoked coherence continued to predict changes in baseline coherence (paired t-test on the distribution of regression slopes: p=1.37e-28; linear regression slopes with p<0.05: 160 out 170 blocks; Figure 7D, see Figure 7—figure supplement 1 for an example session).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of interference stimulation experiments shown in Figure 7D.

claim: The regression parameters for interference stimulation were similar to those obtained with the simple stimulation patterns.
source: Furthermore, the regression parameters were similar to those obtained with the simple stimulation patterns (Figure 6C)
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison of regression parameters across stimulation types.

claim: Both simple and complex stimulation experiments yielded regression slopes that were significantly larger than those obtained from control sessions.
source: and both simple and complex stimulation experiments yielded regression slopes that were significantly larger than those obtained from control sessions (long-latency vs. control sessions, ranksum test: p=0.048; short-latency vs. control sessions, ranksum test: p=0.037; see Figure 7—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical comparison with control sessions shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 2.

claim: There is a robust relationship between stimulus-evoked correlations and changes in baseline connectivity across the network.
source: These results demonstrate a robust relationship between stimulus-evoked correlations and changes in baseline connectivity across the network.
evidence: The claim summarizes the findings from both simple and interference stimulation experiments.

claim: The findings are well explained by a Hebbian model of large-scale stimulation-induced plasticity.
source: These findings are well explained by a Hebbian model of large-scale stimulation-induced plasticity.
evidence: The claim is an interpretation of the experimental results in the context of Hebbian theory.

claim: Functional connectivity between M1 and S1 has been demonstrated in fMRI.
source: Functional connectivity between M1 and S1 has been demonstrated in fMRI (Matsui et al., 2011; McGregor and Gribble, 2015)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior fMRI studies.

claim: Functional connectivity between M1 and S1 has been demonstrated in electrophysiology.
source: Functional connectivity between M1 and S1 has been demonstrated in fMRI (Matsui et al., 2011; McGregor and Gribble, 2015), electrophysiology (Iriki et al., 1989; Yazdan-Shahmorad et al., 2016; Prsa et al., 2017)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior electrophysiology studies.

claim: Functional connectivity between M1 and S1 has been demonstrated in anatomical studies.
source: Functional connectivity between M1 and S1 has been demonstrated in fMRI (Matsui et al., 2011; McGregor and Gribble, 2015), electrophysiology (Iriki et al., 1989; Yazdan-Shahmorad et al., 2016; Prsa et al., 2017), and anatomical studies (Kosar et al., 1985; Petrof et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior anatomical studies.

claim: Variants of SERR have been used previously to evaluate functional connectivity.
source: Variants of SERR (Seeman et al., 2017; Feldmeyer and Sakmann, 2000; Klinshov et al., 2014) and coherence (Bastos and Schoffelen, 2015; Lang et al., 2012) have been used previously to evaluate functional connectivity.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior studies using SERR.

claim: Coherence has been used previously to evaluate functional connectivity.
source: Variants of SERR (Seeman et al., 2017; Feldmeyer and Sakmann, 2000; Klinshov et al., 2014) and coherence (Bastos and Schoffelen, 2015; Lang et al., 2012) have been used previously to evaluate functional connectivity.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior studies using coherence.

claim: SERR and coherence have never been used in combination or compared before this study.
source: However, to our knowledge they have never been used in combination or compared.
evidence: The claim represents a novelty statement about the current study's approach.

claim: SERR is a more direct measure of the projections from the stimulation site.
source: SERR is a more direct measure of the projections from the stimulation site.
evidence: The claim is an interpretation of what SERR measures based on the methodology.

claim: Stimulation likely evokes activity from both terminals and cell bodies located at the stimulation site.
source: Importantly, stimulation likely evokes activity from both terminals and cell bodies located at the stimulation site, though C1V1 does not express well down at the axon (Rajasethupathy et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is based on inference about optogenetic stimulation and supported by citation about C1V1 expression.

claim: C1V1 does not express well down at the axon.
source: though C1V1 does not express well down at the axon (Rajasethupathy et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to prior work on C1V1 expression.

claim: Secondary responses arise from a combination of synaptic, antidromic, and indirect (network) effects.
source: Secondary responses arise from a combination of synaptic, antridromic, and indirect (network) effects.
evidence: The claim is an interpretation of the mechanisms underlying secondary responses.

claim: Based on the timing of the evoked responses and the limited expression of C1V1 in axon terminals, the amplitude of secondary responses normalized to primary response amplitudes is expected to reflect synaptic connectivity.
source: That said, based on the timing of the evoked responses and the limited expression of C1V1 in axon terminals, we expect the amplitude of secondary responses normalized to primary response amplitudes to reflect synaptic connectivity.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on response timing and C1V1 expression patterns.

claim: Coherence measures the broader effects of network-wide dynamics.
source: Coherence, on the other hand, measures the broader effects of network-wide dynamics.
evidence: The claim is an interpretation of what coherence measures.

claim: The correlation between SERR and coherence would be expected in a network where stability was maintained with a Hebbian mechanism.
source: This would be expected in a network where stability was maintained with a Hebbian mechanism.
evidence: The claim is a theoretical expectation based on Hebbian plasticity principles.

claim: Direct connectivity, as reflected in SERR, drives correlated activity, which is reflected in coherence.
source: In other words, direct connectivity, as reflected in SERR, drives correlated activity, which is reflected in coherence
evidence: The claim is an interpretation of the relationship between SERR and coherence based on network dynamics.

claim: Correlated activity drives changes in connectivity.
source: conversely, correlated activity drives changes in connectivity (see Network effects).
evidence: The claim is based on Hebbian plasticity principles.

claim: Coupled mechanisms of connectivity driving correlated activity and correlated activity driving connectivity lead the network to a stable, steady state.
source: These coupled mechanisms lead the network to a stable, steady state (Fox and Stryker, 2017; Toyoizumi et al., 2014; Zenke and Gerstner, 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to theoretical work on network stability.

claim: The decrease in the correlation between SERR and coherence after conditioning seems to be limited to high frequencies.
source: However, this decrease in the correlation between the measures after conditioning seems to be limited to high frequencies and may reflect a transient instability of the network due to the stimulation-induced perturbations in connectivity.
evidence: The claim is an interpretation of the frequency-dependent changes in correlation.

claim: The decrease in correlation between SERR and coherence may reflect a transient instability of the network due to the stimulation-induced perturbations in connectivity.
source: However, this decrease in the correlation between the measures after conditioning seems to be limited to high frequencies and may reflect a transient instability of the network due to the stimulation-induced perturbations in connectivity.
evidence: The claim is a speculative interpretation of the observed decrease in correlation.

claim: Previous work has demonstrated that either activity dependent stimulation can lead to plastic changes in both primate and rodent cortex.
source: Previous work has demonstrated that either activity dependent (Jackson et al., 2006; Lucas and Fetz, 2013; Nishimura et al., 2013; Rebesco et al., 2010; Song et al., 2013) or paired electrical stimulation (Rebesco and Miller, 2011; Seeman et al., 2017) can lead to plastic changes in both primate and rodent cortex.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: Paired electrical stimulation can lead to plastic changes in both primate and rodent cortex.
source: Previous work has demonstrated that either activity dependent (Jackson et al., 2006; Lucas and Fetz, 2013; Nishimura et al., 2013; Rebesco et al., 2010; Song et al., 2013) or paired electrical stimulation (Rebesco and Miller, 2011; Seeman et al., 2017) can lead to plastic changes in both primate and rodent cortex.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: Optogenetic stimulation at even a single location strengthens inter-area functional connectivity between brain areas.
source: Here we demonstrated that optogenetic stimulation at even a single location strengthens inter-area functional connectivity between brain areas.
evidence: The claim summarizes a key finding of the current study.

claim: A similar observation of single-site stimulation strengthening connectivity was reported for one session of single-site electrical stimulation.
source: A similar observation was reported for one session of single-site electrical stimulation (Seeman et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a prior study.

claim: The result that single-site stimulation strengthens inter-area connectivity is consistent with spike-timing dependent plasticity (STDP) rules.
source: This result is consistent with spike-timing dependent plasticity (STDP) rules (Bi and Poo , 2001).
evidence: The claim is an interpretation of the results in the context of STDP theory, supported by citation.

claim: Since the time difference between the activation of the primary (pre-synaptic) and secondary (post-synaptic) responses to optical stimulation is about 3–6 ms, repetitive stimulation should strengthen the connectivity from the site of stimulation to the other area.
source: In particular, since the time difference between the activation of the primary (pre-synaptic) and secondary (post-synaptic) responses to optical stimulation is about 3–6 ms, repetitive stimulation should strengthen the connectivity from the site of stimulation to the other area.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on STDP principles and the observed timing of responses.

claim: Stimulation-induced long-term potentiation (LTP) and STDP have been observed within local circuits.
source: While stimulation-induced long-term potentiation (LTP) and STDP have been observed within local circuits (Iriki et al., 1989; Feldman, 2012; Shulz and Jacob, 2010)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: LTP and STDP have been posited as the mechanism of stimulation-induced plasticity within M1.
source: and have been posited as the mechanism of stimulation-induced plasticity within M1 (Lajoie et al., 2017)
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a modeling study.

claim: This is the first study explaining large-scale changes across cortical networks using Hebbian plasticity.
source: this is the first study explaining large-scale changes across cortical networks.
evidence: The claim represents a novelty statement about the current study's contribution.

claim: The conditioning stimulation frequency (5 or 7 Hz) lies within the range of the theta band.
source: This result is difficult to interpret because the conditioning stimulation frequency (5 or 7 Hz) itself lies within the range of the theta band.
evidence: The claim is a factual statement about the relationship between stimulation frequency and theta band.

claim: It is possible that Hebbian mechanisms are selectively enhancing connectivity at the conditioning frequency.
source: It is possible that Hebbian mechanisms are selectively enhancing connectivity at the conditioning frequency.
evidence: The claim is a speculative interpretation of the theta-band specific effects.

claim: It's possible that theta band coherence best reflects the plastic connections between M1 and S1.
source: It's also possible that theta band coherence best reflects the plastic connections between these areas.
evidence: The claim is a speculative interpretation of the theta-band specific effects.

claim: Neuroplastic changes start almost immediately after the start of stimulation.
source: This trend suggests that neuroplastic changes start almost immediately after the start of stimulation.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the temporal dynamics of connectivity changes.

claim: Unlearning of the stimulation-induced changes was observed during passive recording.
source: Interestingly, we observed unlearning of the stimulation-induced changes during passive recording, though some of the stimulation-induced changes persisted.
evidence: The claim is supported by data showing decreased SERR during baseline recording blocks.

claim: Some of the stimulation-induced changes persisted during passive recording.
source: Interestingly, we observed unlearning of the stimulation-induced changes during passive recording, though some of the stimulation-induced changes persisted.
evidence: The claim is supported by data showing that connectivity did not fully return to baseline.

claim: Previous studies have shown that longer conditioning sessions (3–48 hr) result in changes that are stable over timescales comparable to the length of conditioning.
source: Previous studies have shown that longer conditioning sessions (3–48 hr) result in changes that are stable over timescales comparable to the length of conditioning (Jackson et al., 2006; Lucas and Fetz, 2013; Seeman et al., 2017; Nishimura et al., 2013; Rebesco and Miller, 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: The ability to record artifact-free signals during stimulation allowed testing of the Hebbian model by comparing stimulus-evoked correlations with changes in network correlations.
source: Our ability to record artifact-free signals during stimulation allowed us to perform this test.
evidence: The claim describes a methodological advantage of the optogenetic approach.

claim: There is a predictive linear relationship between stimulus-evoked coherence and the changes in baseline coherence after conditioning.
source: We did find a predictive linear relationship between stimulus-evoked coherence and the changes in baseline coherence after conditioning.
evidence: The claim summarizes a key finding supported by regression analysis in Figures 6 and 7.

claim: The Hebbian model held for both simple and complex spatiotemporal patterns of stimulation-evoked activity.
source: Furthermore, the model held for both simple and complex spatiotemporal patterns of stimulation-evoked activity.
evidence: The claim is supported by data from both non-interference and interference stimulation experiments.

claim: Previous work on sensory cortical plasticity has largely focused on how changes in the statistics of sensory input and/or motor output affect the cortical representation in sensory cortex.
source: First, previous work has largely focused on how changes in the statistics of sensory input and/or motor output affect the cortical representation in sensory cortex.
evidence: The claim describes the focus of prior research in sensory cortical plasticity.

claim: The current study directly manipulated cortical circuits, without a detailed knowledge of the somatotopic map.
source: In contrast, we have directly manipulated cortical circuits, without a detailed knowledge of the somatotopic map.
evidence: The claim describes a key difference between the current study and prior sensory plasticity work.

claim: Earlier work on sensory plasticity studied plasticity on the time scale of days to months.
source: Also, earlier work studied plasticity on the time scale of days to months, while we are studying changes across minutes.
evidence: The claim describes a temporal difference between the current study and prior work.

claim: The current study studied plasticity changes across minutes.
source: Also, earlier work studied plasticity on the time scale of days to months, while we are studying changes across minutes.
evidence: The claim describes the timescale of plasticity studied in the current work.

claim: Both the current study and prior sensory plasticity work appear to support a key role for Hebbian learning in sensorimotor cortical plasticity.
source: Despite these differences, both appear to support a key role for Hebbian learning in sensorimotor cortical plasticity.
evidence: The claim is an interpretation connecting the current findings to prior sensory plasticity literature.

claim: Surface stimulation combined with high blue light absorption and scattering in tissue limits the depth of light penetration.
source: First, surface stimulation combined with high blue light absorption and scattering in tissue limits the depth of light penetration (Yizhar et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim describes a limitation of the experimental approach, supported by citation.

claim: Surface µECoG recordings reflect a summation of nearby neural activity, making comparisons to explicit synaptic learning rules difficult.
source: Second, surface µECoG recordings reflect a summation of nearby neural activity, making comparisons to explicit synaptic learning rules difficult.
evidence: The claim describes a limitation of the recording method.

claim: The results offer a proof-of-concept that optogenetic stimulation can drive predictable changes in network-scale connectivity.
source: Our results offer a proof-of-concept that optogenetic stimulation can drive predictable changes in network-scale connectivity.
evidence: The claim is a summary interpretation of the study's main findings.

claim: The success of optogenetics in NHP represents an important step forward for translational use.
source: The success of optogenetics in NHP represents an important step forward for translational use (Doroudchi et al., 2011; Han, 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations discussing translational potential of optogenetics.

claim: Even where therapeutic approaches ultimately wind up using electrical stimulation, the advantages of optogenetics make it a powerful tool for better understanding the underlying mechanisms of plasticity.
source: However, even where therapeutic approaches ultimately wind up using electrical stimulation, the advantages of optogenetics make it a powerful tool for better understanding the underlying mechanisms of plasticity and, thus, for the development of therapeutic applications of neuromodulation.
evidence: The claim is an interpretation of the value of optogenetics for understanding plasticity mechanisms.

claim: Two adult male rhesus monkeys were used in this study.
source: Two adult male rhesus monkeys (monkey G: 8 years old, 17.5 Kg; monkey J: 7 years old, 16.5 Kg) were used in this study.
evidence: The claim describes the subjects used in the study.

claim: All procedures were performed under the approval of the University of California, San Francisco Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee.
source: All procedures were performed under the approval of the University of California, San Francisco Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee and were compliant with the Guide for the Care and Use of Laboratory Animals.
evidence: The claim describes the ethical approval for the study.

claim: 200 μL of virus was infused in four sites (two in M1 and two in S1) in monkey G.
source: We infused 200 μL of virus in four sites (two in M1 and two in S1) in monkey G
evidence: The claim describes the viral infusion protocol for one monkey.

claim: 250 μL of virus was infused in five sites (two in M1 and three in S1) in monkey J.
source: and 250 μL in five sites (two in M1 and three in S1) of monkey J.
evidence: The claim describes the viral infusion protocol for the other monkey.

claim: Infusion rate started at 1 µl/min and was increased to 5 µl/min.
source: Infusion rate started at 1 µl/min and was increased to 5 µl/min.
evidence: The claim describes the infusion protocol.

claim: In both animals, reliable light evoked neural responses were observed from the large channel-expressing areas.
source: In both animals, we observed reliable light evoked neural responses from the large channel-expressing areas.
